one_line_contribution: That failure-derived memory retrieved from *other* episodes makes an ALFWorld agent re-commit the specific error class it read about, at a rate that rises with the number of verbatim erroneous actions in the item at fixed tokens, and that rewriting the same lesson as a positive corrected procedure keeps the corrective value while removing the imitation — i.e. the value of failure memory sits in write-time framing, not in the presence of failure information.
closest_prior_work: VERIFIED via s2cli (Semantic Scholar): 'Honest Lying: Understanding Memory Confabulation in Reflexive Agents', arXiv:2605.29463 (2026-05-28). Same benchmark (ALFWorld), same phenomenon family, and essentially the same primary metric: it introduces a Reflection Repetition Rate for how often a stored failure-derived reflection's error recurs, reports RRR 0.64 for open-ended self-diagnosis, and concludes that 'reflective memory can reinforce false beliefs rather than correct them'. Critically, its mitigation is a *rewrite of how the note is written* — replacing open-ended self-diagnosis with programmatic extraction of trajectory-level failure signals — which drops RRR to 0.10 and solves 3 of 16 frozen environments. That is the proposal's headline finding (failure memory reproduces the flagged error; changing how the note is written removes it) already demonstrated on the proposal's own benchmark, three months before the proposal, and it is not cited. What survives: 2605.29463 uses self-generated, same-task reflective memory rather than cross-episode retrieval from a stranger's failure, it does not run a content-matched framing factorial (verbatim / negation / positive / contrastive), and it has no dose sweep over verbatim erroneous steps. So the proposal is not fully scooped, but its contribution shrinks to 'the rewrite axis is polarity, and the dose is verbatim error content' rather than 'failure memory drags and rewriting fixes it'. Secondary threats, both verified: Contextual Drag arXiv:2602.04288 (2026-02-04, verified — errors in context produce structurally similar errors across 11 models, mitigations fail) already owns the mechanism in-task; Experience Memory Graph arXiv:2607.13884 (2026-07-15, verified) already builds the positive-corrective form from failed + expert trajectories. From the older in-context-learning line, verified via s2cli: Contrastive Chain-of-Thought arXiv:2311.09277 and 'LLMs can implicitly learn from mistakes in-context' arXiv:2502.08550 both report that invalid/incorrect exemplars in context *help*, and 'Overthinking the Truth' arXiv:2307.09476 gives the false-induction-head account of harmful imitation from bad demonstrations — meaning both directions of the proposal's predicted ordering already have published support in the exemplar setting, and F4 (contrastive) is a rename of a 2023 method.
strongest_objection: Every cell of the predicted ordering is over-determined by two effects that are already established, so no outcome uniquely supports the proposal's causal story, and the one contrast that carries the title is confounded. (a) F1 > none is the expected consequence of in-context copying / false induction heads (arXiv:2307.09476) and of Contextual Drag itself (arXiv:2602.04288); demonstrating it cross-episode is a venue change, not a mechanism. (b) F2 > F3 is exactly what the long-standing negation-comprehension deficit predicts: 'do not X before Y' is harder to follow than 'do Y before X' whether or not any drag exists, and the proposal has no control that separates negation *comprehension* from error *imitation* (e.g. a negation note about an error class with no verbatim command strings versus a positive note with the same content — the plan's action-type paraphrase ablation touches this but is listed only under F2, not run as a factor). (c) The F1-versus-F3 contrast, which carries the abstract's claim that 'the benefit depends on framing rather than on the presence of failure information', is not a framing contrast at all: F1 (verbatim failed excerpt with a FAILED label) contains no statement of the correct action, while F3 (corrected procedure only) does. F3 > F1 is therefore fully explained by F3 containing the answer and F1 not containing it. The stated content-equivalence audit ('same error class, same correction') is internally inconsistent, since F1 by construction has no correction and cannot pass it. Token-matching and neutral filler equalise length, not information. A reviewer will say the study measures 'items that state the right action beat items that do not', which nobody disputes.
what_would_fix_it: Three changes, in order of importance. (1) Run the actual 2x2 the title claims: polarity (negation versus positive) crossed with verbatim-error presence (item quotes the erroneous command strings versus does not), with corrective content held identical in all four cells. That means adding the missing cell — a positively framed item that still quotes the erroneous actions ('the agent did take X before opening Y; the correct step is to open Y first') — and its mirror, a negation note with the prohibition stated only at the action-type level. Only that design can attribute the effect to framing rather than to information content, and only it makes 'the note is the dose' a measurable coefficient rather than a slogan. (2) Position explicitly against arXiv:2605.29463: adopt or subsume its Reflection Repetition Rate, replicate its programmatic-extraction condition as a baseline framing, and state what the framing factorial adds beyond 'a better-written note has lower RRR'. Without this the paper reads as an unacknowledged re-derivation on the same benchmark. (3) Make the claim about *reported benefits* testable: the abstract asserts that 'the benefit reported for failure memory depends on framing', but no published failure-memory system is ever run. Take one system that reports a gain from failure memory (Mistake Notebook arXiv:2512.11485, ExpeL's avoid-style insights, or Reflexion) and swap only the framing of its stored items on the same pool, reporting whether its headline delta moves. That converts a phrasing study into an overturned result, which is what this track's Q8 asks for. Also add a negation-comprehension control and drop or rename F4, which is Contrastive CoT (arXiv:2311.09277) applied to traces.
missing_baseline: The positive-framed item that still contains the verbatim erroneous actions — the fourth cell of the polarity x verbatim-content 2x2. As written the plan has verbatim-plus-negative (F1), abstract-negative (F2), abstract-positive (F3) and F1+F3 concatenated (F4), so verbatim-error presence and negative polarity are perfectly confounded and the dose sweep exists only inside the negatively framed cell. A second omission a reviewer will demand: a matched-success trajectory that *contains the risky step handled correctly* (the plan's S is a generic same-family success, so S versus F1 compares 'no error present' with 'error present' rather than isolating how the same step is presented). Third, no published failure-memory system is run in any condition, so the claim about reported benefits has no baseline at all.
preprint_collision: No verified collision on the exact framing-dose claim, but the check is incomplete in a way that inflates the novelty argument, and it is not neutral. Judgement of the proposal's check: it is more specific than most (named IDs, two channels, honest about exhausting its WebSearch budget, and it correctly rules 2605.24941 out of scope), but it missed the single closest paper, arXiv:2605.29463, which is on ALFWorld, measures failure-derived reflective memory reproducing its own error at 0.64, and fixes it by changing how the note is written — despite the proposal running three ALFWorld-and-failure-memory queries. It also missed the negative-exemplar ICL line (2311.09277, 2502.08550, 2307.09476) that bears directly on F4 and on which direction the ordering should go, and MemoryGraft (2512.16962) on imitation from retrieved cross-episode items. A collision check that misses the nearest same-benchmark neighbour has not established novelty for the claim it is defending.
